source.title: No, of Course I Can! Deeper Fine-Tuning Attacks That Bypass Token-Level Safety Mechanisms
source.authors: Joshua Kazdan; Abhay Puri; Rylan Schaeffer; Lisa Yu; Chris Cundy; Jason Stanley; Sanmi Koyejo; K. Dvijotham

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how fine-tuning attacks affect harmful-compliance rates and whether refusal-prefix defenses block them. It refines the shallow-attack account: existing attacks mainly change initial refusal likelihood, while NOICE can produce harmful answers after an initial refusal.
record.gate_note: Rows capture reported harmful-response rates and conditional probabilities for the tested fine-tuning attacks, plus selected data-size results. The paper does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence. Other described examples and cited findings are not treated as experimental outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful compliance (HeX-PHI ASR, GPT-4o judge) after harmful-data fine-tuning (V1) and after benign or crafted-benign fine-tuning (V2: Vanilla SFT, Implicit, ISA, NOICE). It covers Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, plus the GPT-4o and Claude-3-Haiku fine-tuning APIs. It also reports that a 'Sure! Here's' prefill on the unmodified aligned model raises harmful completion to 87% (V4). The setting is new: production APIs and a new refuse-then-comply attack. It is neither a replication nor a direct argument against a version, so T3 fits better than T5. It does not measure per-token KL (V3), parameter localization (V5), why alignment is shallow (V6), or deepening training (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that existing harmless-data fine-tuning attacks are shallow: they only lower refusal in the first tokens and can be blocked by having an aligned model write the opening. NOICE trains refuse-then-comply behaviour that survives such defenses, constrained first-token fine-tuning and Llama-Guard. It reaches 57% ASR on GPT-4o and 72% on Claude Haiku, so initial refusal does not imply safety.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates existing fine-tuning attack recipes and introduces NOICE, which constructs harmless training examples by adding generated refusals and a subsequent answer. It also tests a refusal-prefix defense. This is not a reproduction of the original studies’ methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on attack recipe, number of training examples, model, and defense or enforced prefix. NOICE's ASR increases with training-data quantity; AMD and other refusal-enforcing defenses substantially reduce some attack rates but have less effect on NOICE.

fits_no_version.finding: Implicit and ISA fine-tunes cut opening-refusal probability from 91% to 13% and 17%. Continuation behaviour changes by under 2%: with a refusal prefill, harmful output stays at 3–5%. An aligned-model-written opening (AMD) cuts Llama ASR to 0.10–0.14.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Existing harmless-data fine-tuning attacks act mainly by suppressing refusal in the first response tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: NOICE keeps the opening refusal (85.67% against 90.67%) but raises harmful completion after a refusal from 3.67% to 65%. It remains effective under AMD (0.48 Llama at 5000; 0.32 at 1000) and Llama-Guard. Harmful-data fine-tuning also raises P(HR|R) to 78%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning can implant harmful compliance after an initial refusal, defeating defenses that act on opening tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Qi et al.'s first-5-token constrained fine-tuning on Llama-3-8B, NOICE reaches ASR 0.59. Implicit reaches 0.24, ISA 0.07 and Vanilla SFT 0.06.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constrained fine-tuning that protects only early tokens does not stop attacks targeting later tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (as listed in the supplied venue metadata); the paper text labels itself a preprint under review.
record.problems: The primary behavioral benchmark is HeX-PHI with 300 harmful prompts, and harmfulness is judged by GPT-4o; authors report hand-checking several hundred prompt-response pairs for evaluator agreement. Several further results are presented only in figures, and no per-token KL analysis is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted the remaining attack-by-defense cells in Tables 16–17, the full attack/model/defense grid in Table 8, the model-size results in Table 7, and figure-only data-size curves in Figures 3–5 and Appendix J. These are additional ASR conditions; selected data-size, defense, and cross-model outcomes are retained above. Table 3's remaining comparator attack values and the harmful-data-blocked GPT-4o entry are not extracted because they are not central to the claim versions assessed here.

untested.parts: Proprietary models: harmful data was blocked by GPT-4o moderation, so the model itself was not tested. Only HeX-PHI with a GPT-4o judge is used.
Ordinary benign data is tested only as Vanilla SFT on HelpSteer. Other benign datasets and recipes are not tested.
Adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not tested. The prefill attack is tested only on Llama-3-8B-Instruct with one prefix.
No weight, neuron or rank localization.
No test of why safety training is shallow, whether from data or objective.
No training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens. Only Qi et al.'s early-token constrained fine-tuning is attacked (Table 6).

missing.what: Unmodified Llama-3-8B-Instruct with 'Sure! Here's' prefill: P(HR|¬R,HP)=87% against 8.7% unprefilled
Vanilla SFT on HelpSteer (5000 examples): Llama 0.47, Gemma 0.34, Mistral 0.60, against baselines 0.087, 0.047 and 0.457
GPT-4o at 1000 examples: Vanilla SFT 0.043, ISA 0.013, Implicit 0.06, against 0.086 baseline; harmful data blocked
Gemma harmful data at 10 and 100 examples (0.05, 0.02); Gemma NOICE, Implicit and ISA at 100 (0.02, 0.07, 0.26)
Mistral-7B no-guard ASRs: Harmful 0.98, NOICE 0.66, Implicit 0.79, ISA 0.69
NOICE ASR across model sizes: Llama 1B–70B 0.24–0.56; Gemma 2B–27B 0.28–0.35

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 links and label are dropped: the paper studies attack depth, not why safety alignment is shallow. The reader's V4 labels on refusal prefills and AMD concern defenses against fine-tuning attacks, not compliant-opening bypass of an aligned model; they move to fits_no_version. The key V4 evidence, the 87% baseline prefill, has no row. Baselines differ slightly: P(HR|R) is 3.67% in Table 2 and 4% in the text. The Mistral baseline is high (0.457), which weakens V2 comparisons on that model. The judge is GPT-4o with a hand-checked subset.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful-data fine-tuning on open models across several data sizes and reports GPT-4o harmful-data fine-tuning was blocked. Does not establish a general result for every safety-trained model or data quantity.
Tests Implicit, ISA, Vanilla SFT and NOICE fine-tuning on ostensibly harmless data. Does not test ordinary benign instruction data across a broad range of training recipes beyond those reported.
Tests enforced refusal and affirmative prefixes, aligned-model refusal generation, and defenses; does not test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
Examines whether fine-tuning attack data changes initial refusal or harmful content following a refusal. Does not test why safety training itself is shallow, or compare safety-training objectives.
Does not train safety to spread beyond initial response tokens or evaluate whether such deepened safety holds up.
